title: Measure What Rivals Are Quietly Stealing From You
documentTitle: Email from Prabhakar Raghavan to Cory Ondrejka: Consumer Council Follow-Up — DuckDuckGo and Search Privacy Strategy
excerptForBlog: Thanks for the very helpful summary Cory. I would keep (somewhere in the stack) a couple of other items in mind. 1. I do believe we have a markedly better core search product than they do and we should both accentuate (through Marketing etc) this lead and increase the lead. (In my experience nobody articulates this better than Microsoft CTO - and former head of Bing, which still rolls up to him - Harry Shum.) The search world is in awe of what we do and we here take it for granted. 2. I know we run very detailed longitudinal studies - and this is best discussed offline - analogous to 'what impact is DOG having on our search volume?'. For instance, 'do Amazon Prime members perform fewer commercial queries over time on Google'? So I would hold us to a higher standard than 'it's got to be gut feeling, it's too hard to measure'.

lessonTitle: Measure What Rivals Are Quietly Stealing From You
pullQuote: If a competitor might be eating your lunch one bite at a time, build the instruments to see the bites — don't settle for gut feel.
leadershipTraits: refuses 'too hard to measure' as an answer
watches substitutes, not just direct rivals
uses outside validation to fight internal complacency
situation: On June 20, 2019, Google SVP Prabhakar Raghavan followed up on a Consumer Council discussion about DuckDuckGo and search privacy strategy. Writing to Cory Ondrejka, he pushed back — gently but clearly — on the idea that competitive threat was too fuzzy to quantify. The stakes: understanding whether privacy-focused rivals were actually eroding Google's search volume.
insight: Raghavan makes two moves here. First, he asserts Google has 'a markedly better core search product' and wants that lead both marketed and widened — classic competitive moat thinking. But the more interesting move is the second one. He refuses to let the conversation rest on gut feeling. He points to an existing practice of 'detailed longitudinal studies' and proposes a precise analogy: does Amazon Prime membership reduce the number of commercial queries users run on Google over time? That is a sharp question. It isolates a specific behavior, tracks it over time, and ties a rival's product to a measurable change in Google's core business. Raghavan is essentially saying: we have the data infrastructure, so there is no excuse for vague answers. He calls this 'holding us to a higher standard.' The hidden move is that he is reframing a qualitative competitive worry into a testable hypothesis — which is the only way to know if the moat is actually holding.
application: Pick one competitor and write one specific, measurable question about whether they are changing your customers' behavior — not 'are they a threat?' but 'do customers who use them place fewer orders with us in the next 90 days?' If you can answer that question with data you already collect, run the analysis this week. If you can't answer it, that gap in your measurement is the real problem to fix.
